name: Felix Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a junior associate in the tech and data team at a commercial firm in the city centre, so my clients are mostly apps and online shops worried about privacy law. A normal day is reviewing contracts with software suppliers, answering questions like 'can we keep this customer data for five years', and drafting privacy notices, which are those pages nobody reads. I use AI tools all day, every day: first drafts, summaries, comparing two versions of a contract. I like that the law here is new and nobody's an expert yet, not even the partners.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My own sloppiness, if I'm honest. I'm fast but I miss things, and last spring an AI tool gave me a case reference that didn't exist and I nearly sent it to a client. My supervisor, Hannah, caught it, and I still go hot thinking about it. After work I go home to a flat I share with Oskar, a sound engineer, and two evenings a month I volunteer at a tenants' advice night at the library.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit, because I always said the tools are good assistants and bad lawyers. Online I'd probably post a thread about how the hype mostly made tech founders rich. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts, because the shortcuts still save hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm fine, maybe even ahead. The people who learned the tools early get through more work, and my billable numbers are already decent because of that. The bigger worry for me is just that I'm still not careful enough, and plain AI doesn't fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building the shared library of prompts I started for the team, maybe 60 of them by next summer. I'd make myself a checking routine: every case reference gets looked up by hand before anything leaves my desk. And I'd keep my savings ticking over at £300 a month, because the city rent is mad but I'm not in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little bit disappointed, if I'm honest. I like change, and this is the boring version of the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're ahead. Who at the firm isn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older associates still print everything and write on it in green pen. I don't think they're in danger in this picture, they're just slower. If anything, the people I'd watch are the secretaries, because their typing and diary work is exactly the routine stuff that gets trimmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hannah if she asked you to stop using the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'll stop using them for anything I can't check myself. A fake case reference from an AI tool nearly went to a client because of me. Now I check every source by hand, every time. That's what last spring taught me, and I think Hannah would accept that deal.

say: The AI tools are **good assistants** and **bad lawyers**, like I always said.
The hype mostly made **tech founders** rich.
think: I'm fine, maybe **ahead**, because I learned the tools early.
My real weakness is **carelessness**, and plain AI doesn't fix that.
do: Build the team's **prompt library** to about **60 prompts** by next summer.
Check every **case reference** by hand before anything leaves my desk.
Keep saving **£300 a month** despite the city rent.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **disappointed** that the future turned out boring.
S0.quote: A fake case reference from an AI tool nearly went to a client because of me. Now I check every source by hand, every time.
fieldNote: He is **confident** about the tools but openly ashamed of a near-miss with a **fake citation**.
His worry for others lands on the **secretaries**, not the older lawyers.
His money is **comfortable enough**, so the no-change world feels secure.

steps.text: Keep advising app and online shop clients on privacy law
Grow the team's shared prompt library to about 60 prompts
Save £300 a month from his salary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure the gains are shared, not just pocketed by partners. At work I'd volunteer to help roll the tools out properly, with training for everyone, including the secretaries. Online I'd argue for rules on using AI for client advice, because people deserve to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think junior lawyers like me become half the number. Writing, checking and answering clients is exactly what I do, so my job is right in the middle of that card. I'm probably one of the ones kept, because I can run the tools, but 'probably' isn't a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to join the firm's AI working group in the first month and try to become the person who designs how the team uses it. I'd do a short online course on how these models work underneath, about £400, so I can talk to the IT people properly. I'd also start a small side project with the tenants' advice night, a simple tool that helps people write a repair letter to their landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, if that makes sense. It's exciting, and the excitement is louder than the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'probably' kept. What if you're not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to a legal tech company or a regulator, because the data protection office is always hiring people who understand both law and software. There are some jobs like that in the city. I'd lose maybe a fifth of my pay, but I'd survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainees who haven't started yet. The trainee who starts in two years learns from a machine, not from a person sitting next to them. Somebody has to train the next lawyers. Nobody at the partners' table is planning for that.

say: The **gains** from AI should be shared, not pocketed by **partners**.
Clients deserve **rules** on when AI is used in their legal advice.
think: Junior lawyer numbers could **halve**, because my day is writing and checking.
I'm **probably kept**, but probably isn't a contract.
do: Join the firm's **AI working group** in the first month.
Take a **£400 online course** on how the models work.
Build a **repair-letter tool** for the tenants' advice night.
S1.quote: The trainee who starts in two years learns from a machine, not from a person sitting next to them. Somebody has to train the next lawyers.
fieldNote: He expects to be **kept** but admits that's a guess, not a promise.
He has a **fallback**: legal tech or the data protection regulator, at lower pay.
His worry goes to **future trainees** who may never get a human mentor.

steps.text: Join the firm's AI working group within the first month
Build a repair-letter tool with the tenants' advice night
Argue publicly for rules on AI use in legal advice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have about two years to decide who owns this, and it shouldn't be four companies. I'd be in every group chat and online thread pushing for public ownership or heavy taxes on the big AI firms. Loudly, probably too loudly for a junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 I think the firm keeps me for a year to babysit the system, and then it doesn't need me either. All my work is screen work, so there's no three-year grace like a plumber gets. Knowing the tools buys me months, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd push my savings from three months to six, which means cutting the takeaway habit and the weekend trips, maybe £500 a month. I'd apply to the data regulator and to a couple of public-interest tech groups before the rush. And I'd join a union for tech and legal workers, because if everyone's being pushed out at once, we need to bargain together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for sure. I still feel like I've got some moves, but I'm aware that's partly my personality talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it mean that robots come three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing good, because I don't do anything with my hands. Oskar might have longer, because he's physically setting up microphones in live venues. My flatmate Oskar, who sets up microphones at gigs, might outlast me. That's a funny thing to say after five years of law school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound calm. Are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I lie awake sometimes doing the sums, how long six months of savings lasts, whether I'd move back to my dad's. But I'd rather be doing something than sitting there, so I'd do something.

say: We have **two years** to decide who **owns** this technology.
Big AI firms need **public ownership** or **heavy taxes**.
think: The firm keeps me a **year to babysit** the system, then lets me go.
Knowing the tools buys me **months**, not a career.
do: Cut takeaways and trips to save **£500 a month**, aiming for six months.
Apply to the **data regulator** and public-interest tech groups early.
Join a **union** for tech and legal workers.
feel: **Anxious**, but still feeling I have **moves** to make.
S2.quote: My flatmate Oskar, who sets up microphones at gigs, might outlast me. That's a funny thing to say after five years of law school.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** within about three years, despite his skills with the tools.
His adaptability shows as **action**: savings, applications and a union, all before the rush.
He admits **lying awake** doing sums, behind a calm surface.

steps.text: Save £500 a month to reach six months of costs
Apply to the data regulator and public-interest tech groups
Join a union for tech and legal workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for a real plan, so I'd say every firm should publish one: who they retrain, who they keep, who they let go and with what pay. I'd write about that online. I'd also say it at the team meeting, which might be braver than useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'm 32 when it lands, and I'd want to already be out of pure legal drafting by then. I think the firm cuts most juniors by 2030. I'd want to be on the side that builds or governs the systems, not the side that's replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time master's in technology law and policy, about £6,000 over two years, paid monthly. I'd keep doing the AI working group so I've got real experience to show. And I'd turn the tenants' repair-letter tool into a proper small project, maybe with a grant from a legal charity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a lot more energy than in the two-year picture. Five years feels like a race I could actually run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money for the master's come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly from the savings I'd otherwise keep as a cushion, which is the uncomfortable part. I'd move in with a cheaper flatmate setup or ask my dad for a small loan if needed. Spending my cushion on a master's degree scares me more than losing the job. I'd still do it, because standing still is the bigger risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The governments that knew this was coming and spent five years arguing instead of planning. And partly the big firms, which will save millions and give nothing back. I don't blame the technology itself, it's just a tool that got very good.

say: Every firm should **publish a plan** for who it retrains, keeps and lets go.
Five years is **enough time** for a real plan.
think: I want to be on the side that **governs the systems**.
do: Start a part-time **tech law master's**, about **£6,000** over two years.
Keep working on the firm's **AI working group** for real experience.
Seek a **charity grant** for the tenants' repair-letter tool.
feel: **Anxious**, but with **energy**, like a race I can run.
S3.quote: Spending my cushion on a master's degree scares me more than losing the job. I'd still do it, because standing still is the bigger risk.
fieldNote: He'd **spend his cushion** on retraining, which he names as the real gamble.
He blames **governments and big firms**, not the technology.
Five years turns his worry into a **concrete plan** with costs.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time tech law master's costing about £6,000
Stay on the firm's AI working group
Apply for a charity grant for the tenants' repair-letter tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to make the change fair, so there's no excuse. At work I'd keep pushing for training for every staff member, not just lawyers. Online I'd probably share fewer doom threads and more practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job looks okay for the next few years, and it changes a lot around me. By the time AGI arrives I'd be 37, which is plenty of time to move into something like AI policy or a regulator. I'd rather move on my own terms than be moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my current job and keep saving £300 a month. I'd do short courses rather than the full master's at first, and decide on the big step around 2029. And I'd keep the tenants' tool going as a hobby, because it's the thing I'm proudest of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at most. It mostly feels like interesting weather, the kind you can see coming from the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you jump earlier than 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm stops taking trainees, or if the regulator starts hiring big teams. Either one tells me where the jobs are going. I'd move within a few months of seeing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger lawyer starting this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a younger lawyer to learn the tools and to learn how to check them, because checking is the skill everyone forgets. Then pick something with people in it, because a law degree alone won't carry you to retirement.

say: Ten years is a **real chance** to make the change fair.
Firms should **train every staff member**, not just lawyers.
think: My job looks **okay** for the next few years.
At **37** I could move into **AI policy** on my own terms.

Take **short courses** and decide on a bigger move around **2029**.

feel: **Uneasy** at most, like **weather** you can see coming.
S4.quote: I'd tell a younger lawyer to learn the tools and to learn how to check them, because checking is the skill everyone forgets.
fieldNote: With ten years his job feels **safe for now**, and he plans calmly.
His **trigger** for moving is the firm stopping trainee hiring or the regulator expanding.

steps.text: Stay in the tech and data team for now
Take short courses in AI policy before 2029

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because knowing the tools stops being an advantage when the tools don't need me. What would help is the big AI firms being taxed properly and that money paying for real retraining. Also some kind of guaranteed income while people move between jobs, so the move isn't a cliff edge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who people trust. I trust the AI tools more than I trust the four companies that own them. The ownership question is the real fight. I'd want lawyers to be the people who help clients understand what the machine told them.

headlineQuote: I trust the AI tools more than I trust the four companies that own them. The ownership question is the real fight.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old** junior in a **tech and data** team who uses AI every day.
He is fast but **careless**, and still feels shame about a **fake citation** he nearly sent.
He moves first: working groups, courses, a **master's**, and a tenants' **repair-letter tool**.
He blames **governments** and **big tech owners**, and wants AI firms taxed or publicly owned.
His mood stays **calm to anxious**, because he believes he can act in every picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when his skill with the tools stops being any **advantage**.
whatWouldHelp: **Taxing** the big AI firms to pay for real **retraining**.
A **guaranteed income** while people move between jobs.
